title: Taking the hukam
hookLine: the Granth is opened at random and the first hymn on the left page read

cards: Nobody picks the page. That's the first thing to know. The Granth has been opened at dawn, and now the reader sits behind it, hands resting on the cloth.
The sangat waits. The reader doesn't flip to a favorite hymn or a passage that suits the news. The Granth is opened where it opens.
Then the reader's eyes go to one particular place on the page, and whatever is written there is read aloud to everyone in the hall.
It has a name, and some gurdwaras write it on a board by the door for anyone who missed it.

teach.b: This has come up twice already, with the Tenth Guru's letters and with the one line carried through a day. Today, the method. The word is hukam: order, command.
What's read is called the hukam, or the hukamnama, the written order. In paraphrase, the code gives the method. Open the Granth at random.

teach.h: THE LEFT PAGE, FROM THE HYMN'S START.
teach.b: Read the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. If that hymn began on the page before, turn back and read it from its beginning. The hymn is read whole, not cut off where the page happens to start.
Because the word hukam goes back to the very first page of the Granth. Japji Sahib asks how a person can become truthful, how the wall of falsehood can be broken.
And it answers, in paraphrase: by walking in the hukam, the Will, which is written along with us. So for Sikhs, hukam isn't a boss's memo.

It's the Will that orders everything, the way the tide is ordered and the seasons are. The daily hukam is a small, concrete window onto that: one hymn, received rather than chosen, heard as the Guru's word for this day.
It's easy to mistake this for fortune-telling, and that's not how it's understood. The hukam doesn't predict anything.

teach.h: NOT A FORECAST: THE GURU SPEAKS.
teach.b: For Sikhs, every page of the Granth is the Guru's word, so wherever it opens, the Guru speaks. What changes is the listening. Some Sikhs read the day's hukam from a gurdwara on their phone before work.

how: After the Granth is opened in the morning, the granthi opens it at random and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page as the hukam; some gurdwaras display it by the door or share it online.

practice: If you can, find today's hukam from a gurdwara and read it slowly, once; if not, take any line of scripture or wisdom you didn't choose, from a book opened where it falls.
Let one phrase stay, and hold it as if it were addressed to today, and only today.

wordCard.voice: Taking the hukam. Opening the Granth at random and reading the first hymn on the left-hand page, from its beginning: the Guru's order for the day. Today's word.

orig.note: Punjabi: order, command; in Japji Sahib, the divine Will.

carryVoice: Your line: the order of the day. Received, not chosen, and heard for this day only. See you tomorrow.
